# Booth et al., NIST SP 800-218A (secure development practices for generative AI and dual-use foundation models), Warranting Agent-Built Software Distillation

**Source:** Harold Booth, Murugiah Souppaya, Apostol Vassilev, Michael Ogata, Martin Stanley and Karen Scarfone, *Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile*, NIST Special Publication 800-218A, July 2024, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218A. Not subject to copyright in the United States (Authority, PDF p. 3). **Scope:** open. Citations take the form `(task ID, p. N)`, printed page numbers, with item IDs such as `PW.1.1.C2` where one recommendation (R), consideration (C) or note (N) is meant.

**Setting, read before projecting.** The Profile is a companion to SSDF 1.1 (`nist-ssdf-1-1`) for organisations that develop AI models, build software on top of them, or buy such software. Its subject is the *model* as a thing being built: its training data, weights, pipelines, testing and integration into other software. It is not about coding agents writing software, and it puts the deployment and operation of AI systems out of scope. It reaches this axis by two routes. Directly, when a change adds a model feature (an LLM call, a prompt, a tool, a vendor model), the builder becomes what the Profile calls an AI system producer, and its tasks apply as written. By transfer, its one statement about AI-written code (it does not distinguish human-written from AI-generated source code, because all code should be evaluated before use) and its controls on development environments carry across to the coding agent's own sandbox. Every transfer is marked as one below. The Profile's items are recommendations, considerations and notes inside a risk-based starting point, not requirements; this distillation keeps that hedge.

**Applicability gate (Pass G.0): clear yes.** (1) The source answers practitioner questions this axis asks: what a model feature touches and which tasks that makes necessary, what the agent can reach, which claims are backed by a tool's artifact, and what the warranty pack must say it did not cover. (2) Its practices land on seven of the eight phases, strongest on triaging the risk of model features, gating on recorded evidence and warranting. Phase 1 gets only model-feature requirements; nothing in it speaks to acceptance criteria. (3) Its contrarian positions (not a checklist; not to be used without SP 800-218; no separate bar for AI-generated code) bear directly on how a builder selects and evidences the gates.

**Phase mapping.**

| Phase | Fit | What the source brings |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Specifying the change | Partial | For a model feature only: AI model security in the requirements (PO.1.2), forms of model documentation, requirements passed to third parties (PO.1.3), and who does which task when a vendor's model is involved. Nothing on acceptance criteria or non-goals |
| 2 Triaging risk | Strong (model features) | AI threat types in risk modelling (PW.1.1.R1); no model on a critical security path without a human (PW.1.1.C2); human approval beyond risk-based thresholds (PO.4.1.C1); priorities and risk-based task selection; models trained on sensitive data (PS.3.2.R2); the cybersecurity-only limit |
| 3 Locking the tests | Partial | AI models brought under testing policy, with named test types, regression automation and retesting after retraining (PW.8); adversarial samples (PW.3.3). Nothing on who writes the tests or on tests edited to pass |
| 4 Building in the sandbox | Moderate, partly by transfer | Separated and protected environments, least privilege, plaintext-secrets monitoring, production data only in approved environments (PO.5.1); continuous monitoring with alerts (PO.5.3); acquired components verified before use (PW.4.4); input and output handling (PW.5.1) |
| 5 Gating deterministically | Moderate | Toolchains that generate artifacts as evidence (PO.3); criteria for security checks tracked (PO.4.1); every issue recorded and triaged (PW.7.2); model scans; secure serialisation; hashes and signatures (PS.2.1); waivers justified (PW.1) |
| 6 Reviewing independently | Moderate | Design review by a qualified person not involved in the design *and* by automation (PW.2.1); review or analysis chosen by policy (PW.7.1); one bar for AI-generated and human code (p. 2); root causes analysed for patterns (RV.3.2) |
| 7 Warranting the change | Strong | Artifacts as evidence; per-party responsibility and attestation; documenting what the practices did not cover and data of unknown provenance; a selection record, since it is no checklist; retained documentation (PS.3.1); the cybersecurity-only limit |
| 8 Releasing and operating | Partial, scope-limited | Deployment and operation are out of scope. The Respond to Vulnerabilities practices still apply: logged inputs and outputs, reporting channels, vulnerability-database watch including ML frameworks, frequent scanning, stop-and-rollback criteria, root cause and class sweeps (RV.1–RV.3) |

## Warranting Agent-Built Software Relevance

The Profile gives an accountable builder the security task list for the moment a change puts a model inside the software, and a small number of rules that hold for agent-built software in general. Its starting point is that AI models and systems "inherit much of the same risk as any other digital system" [V] and bring new risk besides: "A unique challenge for this community is the blurring of traditional boundaries between system code and system data, as well as the use of plain human language as the means of interaction with the systems." [V] (p. 1). For a change that adds an LLM call, a prompt or a tool, that sentence is the reason the triage phase cannot stop at the code: the data the model reads and the words a user types are part of the attack surface. The Profile's Table 1 turns this into named tasks with suggested priorities: AI threat types in risk modelling, a human where a model would otherwise make a significant security decision, integrity and provenance checks on acquired models, careful input and output handling, models brought under scanning and testing, and criteria for when to stop using a model and roll back.

For the warranty pack itself, three of its positions carry the weight. It is "not a checklist to follow" [V] (p. 4), so a pack that claims conformance has to show which tasks were selected for this change and why. It asks organisations to write down what their practices did not cover, and, where a model from another party is involved, which party is responsible for each task and how each attests (pp. 4–5). And it treats AI-generated source code no differently from human-written code, because all of it should be evaluated before use (p. 2): the agent's code does not get a lighter bar for being machine-written, nor a separate one. Its limits matter as much: it addresses cybersecurity only, puts deployment and operation out of scope, and is written for model development rather than for agents that build software, so the agentic and operational sides of the harness need other sources in this corpus.

## Key Concepts for Warranting Agent-Built Software

1. <!-- concept: risk-based-starting-point-not-checklist --> **A risk-based starting point, not a checklist.** "The SSDF Community Profile is not a checklist to follow, but rather a starting point for planning and implementing a risk-based approach to adopting secure software development practices involving AI models." [V] (p. 4). Organisations weigh risk, cost, feasibility and applicability in choosing tasks, and may adapt, customise and omit items [AR] (pp. 4, 6). Priority (High, Medium, Low) "is intended to be a starting point for organizations to assign their own priorities" [V] (p. 6). It should not be used without SP 800-218 (p. 1). For the harness: the selection of tasks for a change is itself a record the pack carries.

2. <!-- concept: one-bar-for-ai-generated-code --> **One bar for AI-generated and human-written code.** The Profile does not distinguish the two, "because it is assumed that all source code should be evaluated for vulnerabilities and other issues before use" [V] (p. 2). The only direct statement in the source about AI-written code, and it cuts both ways: the agent's output gets no exemption, and the Profile asks for no extra scrutiny beyond what all code gets. It does not say the evaluation must be a human reading (see Concept 6).

3. <!-- concept: ai-threat-types-in-risk-modelling --> **AI threat types in risk modelling.** PW.1.1 (High) uses threat modelling, attack modelling or attack surface mapping; R1 adds AI-specific types, citing NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy [BT]: poisoning of training data, malicious code or other unwanted content in inputs and outputs, denial of service from adversarial prompts, supply chain attacks, unauthorised information disclosure, theft of model weights, and misconfigured data pipelines; C1 considers updating the risk model for later model versions (PW.1.1, pp. 13–14) [AP]. The Introduction adds that crafted user queries can produce objectionable output or, unsanitised, drive injection-style attacks (p. 1) [AR].

4. <!-- concept: human-on-security-decisions --> **A human where the model would decide security.** During risk modelling, consider checking that the model is not on a critical path for significant security decisions without a human in the loop (PW.1.1.C2, p. 14) [AP]; consider human review and approval for security checks beyond risk-based thresholds (PO.4.1.C1, p. 10) [AP]; for ongoing scanning and testing, rely mainly on automation and bring in a human as needed (RV.1.2.R2, p. 18) [AP]. These are considerations (C items, "something the organization should consider doing" [V], p. 6) except the last, a recommendation.

5. <!-- concept: artifacts-as-evidence --> **Toolchains that generate artifacts as evidence.** PO.3 uses automation to improve the accuracy, reproducibility and comprehensiveness of security practices and to document and demonstrate their use (p. 9) [AP]. PO.3.1.N1: ideally, automated toolchains will do the vast majority of the work of securing AI model development (p. 9) [AP]. PO.3.3 configures tools to generate artifacts of their support for the practices; N1 defines an artifact as an item of evidence, and evidence as grounds for belief or disbelief, citing other NIST publications [BT] (p. 10). An agent's summary is not such an artifact; a tool's record is.

6. <!-- concept: record-and-triage-every-finding --> **Code review or analysis, and every finding recorded and triaged.** PW.7.1 decides whether code review (a person looks at the code) and/or code analysis (tools find issues) is used, by policy; R1 brings AI model code into that policy (p. 16) [AP]. PW.7.2 (High) performs it and records and triages all discovered issues and recommended remediations in the team's workflow or issue tracker; R1 scans all AI models for malware, vulnerabilities and backdoors (pp. 16–17) [AP]. PW.8.2 does the same for test results (p. 17) [AP].

7. <!-- concept: ai-models-under-test-policy --> **AI models under the testing policy.** PW.8.1.R1 includes AI models in code testing policies, naming unit, integration, penetration, red-team, use case and adversarial testing; C1 considers automating tests in the pipeline as regression tests (p. 17) [AP]. PW.8.2.R2: retest models when they are retrained or new data sources are added (p. 17) [AP]. PW.3.3 includes adversarial samples in training and testing data, under controls (p. 15) [AP].

8. <!-- concept: separated-protected-environments --> **Separated, protected, watched environments.** PO.5.1 (High): C1 considers separating execution environments by isolation, segmentation, containment or access via APIs; R2 stores sensitive data used in model development, including production data, only in organisation-approved environments; R3 applies least privilege to pipelines and registries; "Continuously monitor each environment for plaintext secrets." [V] (PO.5.1.R6, p. 11). PO.5.3 (High, new) monitors development environments continuously and alerts when activity passes a risk threshold (p. 11) [AP]. PS.1.1 keeps all forms of code, including configuration-as-code, on least privilege (pp. 11–12) [AP]. Applying these to a coding agent's sandbox is a transfer: the Profile writes them for the environments where models are developed.

9. <!-- concept: verify-acquired-ai-components --> **Acquired components verified before use.** PW.4.4 (High) verifies that third-party components comply with requirements throughout their life cycles; R1 verifies the integrity, provenance and security of an acquired model and its datasets, adapters and configuration before use; R2 scans and thoroughly tests them for vulnerabilities and malicious content (pp. 15–16) [AP]. PS.3.2 tracks provenance of the model, its components and the libraries and pipelines used to build it (p. 13) [AP]; PS.2.1 provides hashes or signatures for a model, its components and its changes (p. 12) [AP]; PW.6.1.C1 considers secure model serialisation (p. 16) [AP].

10. <!-- concept: design-review-person-and-automation --> **Design review by an uninvolved person and by automation.** PW.2.1 (High, modified from SSDF 1.1) has 1) a qualified person or people not involved with the design and 2) automated processes in the toolchain review the design to confirm and enforce that it meets all security requirements and addresses the identified risk (p. 14) [AP]. Both, not either; see the integration table.

11. <!-- concept: shared-responsibility-and-uncovered-parts --> **Shared responsibility, and what the practices did not cover.** Where one party's model runs in another's system, "there is likely a shared responsibility model" [V] (p. 5), and the acquirer can set out "which party is responsible for each practice and task and how each party will attest to its conformance with the agreement" [V] (p. 5). Because final weights exist only after training, some parts resist secure-development practices: "Organizations should document the parts and artifacts that are not covered by the secure software development practices." [V] (p. 4). PW.3.2 documents data that lack known provenance (p. 15) [AP].

12. <!-- concept: stop-and-rollback-criteria --> **Criteria to stop using a model, and root causes after.** RV.2.2.R2 sets criteria and processes for when to stop using a model and when to roll back to a previous version (p. 18) [AP]; C1: "Consider being prepared to stop using an AI model at any time and to continue operations through other means until the AI model’s risks are sufficiently addressed." [V] (p. 19). RV.3 analyses root causes, looks for patterns over time, sweeps for the same class, and updates the development process so the cause does not recur (p. 19) [AP].

## Questions to Ask During Warranting Agent-Built Software

### Phase 1: Specifying the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Model security in the requirements | If this change adds a model feature, are its security requirements written down alongside the rest, from laws, contracts and standards as well as policy? | PO.1.2.R1, p. 8 |
| Data classification | Does the existing data classification cover what the model will read and write, or does it need extending? | PO.1.2.C1, p. 8 |
| Model documentation | Is there a data, model or system card (or equivalent) for the model this change uses? | PO.1.2.N1, p. 8 |
| Third parties | Have the model's security requirements been passed to the vendor supplying it? | PO.1.3.R1, p. 8 |
| Who does what | Where a vendor's model sits in the change, is it written which party does each task and how each attests? | p. 5 |

### Phase 2: Triaging risk

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Threat types | Has the risk model for this change been run against the AI threat types: unwanted content in inputs and outputs, adversarial prompts, supply chain, information disclosure, poisoned data, misconfigured pipelines? | PW.1.1.R1, pp. 13–14 |
| Security decisions | Would the model's output decide a security question (access, approval, closing an alert) with no human step? | PW.1.1.C2, p. 14 |
| Thresholds | Which security checks on this change pass the risk threshold at which a human must review and approve? | PO.4.1.C1, p. 10 |
| Task selection | Which of the Profile's tasks apply to this kind of change, at what priority of our own, and where is that choice recorded? | p. 4; p. 6 |
| Sensitive training data | Is the model trained or fine-tuned on personal, payment or health data, and should access to it then be limited to those who may see that data? | PS.3.2.R2, p. 13 |
| Other risks | Privacy, intellectual property and bias are outside this source: who is handling them for this change? | p. 5 |

### Phase 3: Locking the tests

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Test types | For the model feature, which of unit, integration, penetration, red-team, use case and adversarial testing does the risk call for? | PW.8.1.R1, p. 17 |
| Regression | Are the model's tests automated in the pipeline so they run on every change? | PW.8.1.C1, p. 17 |
| Retraining | Was the model retrained, fine-tuned or given a new data source since its tests last ran? | PW.8.2.R2, p. 17 |
| Data before use | Was the new training or test data checked for integrity, provenance and signs of poisoning before use? | PW.3.1, pp. 14–15 |

### Phase 4: Building in the sandbox

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Separation | Is the agent's environment separated from the others (isolation, segmentation, containment, API-only access)? (transfer) | PO.5.1.C1, p. 10 |
| Production data | Is any production data, or an extract of it, sitting in the sandbox, a fixture or a test database? (transfer) | PO.5.1.R2, p. 10 |
| Secrets | Is something watching the environment for plaintext secrets, continuously? | PO.5.1.R6, p. 11 |
| Least privilege | Can the agent change code, configuration-as-code or the toolchain beyond what its task needs? (transfer) | PS.1.1, pp. 11–12; PO.3.2.R2, p. 9 |
| New components | Was every component or model the agent brought in verified for integrity, provenance and security before use? | PW.4.4, pp. 15–16 |
| Untrusted input | Are the feature's inputs (prompts, user data) logged, validated and sanitised, and its outputs encoded so they cannot execute? | PW.5.1.R2–R3, p. 16 |

### Phase 5: Gating deterministically

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | Does each gate result come from a tool-generated artifact, or from someone's account of it? | PO.3.3, p. 10 |
| Criteria | What are this change's criteria for its security checks, and are they tracked through the build? | PO.4.1, p. 10 |
| Findings | Is every issue the scans and tests found recorded and triaged in the tracker, including the suppressed ones? | PW.7.2, pp. 16–17 |
| Model artifacts | Was the model scanned for malware, vulnerabilities and backdoors, and is it loaded through a secure serialisation format? | PW.7.2.R1, p. 17; PW.6.1.C1, p. 16 |
| Integrity | Do the model and its components carry hashes or signatures that the release can be checked against? | PS.2.1, p. 12 |
| Waivers | Where a requirement was relaxed or a check waived, where is the justification? | PW.1, pp. 13–14 |

### Phase 6: Reviewing independently

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Independence | Was the design reviewed by a qualified person not involved in it, *and* by automated checks? | PW.2.1, p. 14 |
| Review or analysis | For this code, did policy call for human review, tool analysis or both, and was that done? | PW.7.1, p. 16 |
| Same bar | Is the agent's code evaluated the way human code is, no lighter? | p. 2 |
| History | Has the root-cause record for this area been checked for patterns, and the change for the same class of defect? | RV.3.2–RV.3.3, p. 19 |

### Phase 7: Warranting the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Demonstrated | Which claims in the pack rest on a tool's artifact, and which only on a report? | PO.3.3, p. 10; PW.8.2, p. 17 |
| Selection | If the pack claims conformance with this Profile or SSDF, does it show which tasks were selected and why? | p. 4 |
| Not covered | Does the pack list the parts and artifacts the practices did not cover, and the data of unknown provenance? | p. 4; PW.3.2, p. 15 |
| Vendor split | For a vendor model, does the pack say what the vendor attests to and what we do? | p. 5 |
| Retained record | Is the reason the model was chosen kept with the release? | PS.3.1.R2, p. 13 |
| Scope | Does the pack say that its security evidence does not cover privacy, intellectual property or bias? | p. 5 |

### Phase 8: Releasing and operating

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Stop criteria | What would make us stop using this model, and how does the product keep working without it? | RV.2.2.R2, C1, pp. 18–19 |
| Watching | Are the model's inputs and outputs logged and analysed for security and performance issues? | RV.1.1.R1, p. 17 |
| Reporting | Do users of the model know how to report a security problem and what its limits are? | RV.1.1.R2, p. 17; RV.1.3.R2, p. 18 |
| Dependencies | Is someone watching vulnerability and incident databases for the ML frameworks and libraries the product uses? | RV.1.1.R3, p. 18 |
| Ongoing scanning | Are the models scanned and tested often, mainly by automation, with periodic audits? | RV.1.2, p. 18 |

## What to Look For

| Signal | Diagnosis | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| The pack says *SSDF compliant* or *follows 800-218A* and lists no tasks | The Profile used as a checklist badge, which it says it is not; a conformance claim with no selection behind it (p. 4) | Return the pack for the task-selection record: which tasks, at what priority, and why the rest were left out |
| A model's output closes, grants or approves something security-relevant on its own | A model on a critical security path without a human (PW.1.1.C2) | Put a human step in, or record why the risk model says one is not needed |
| A gate's result is the agent's sentence, not the tool's output | No artifact; the claim is a report (PO.3.3) | Rerun the gate so it writes its own record, and attach that |
| Findings from a scan or review sit in a chat transcript | Issues not recorded and triaged in the tracker (PW.7.2) | Move each to the tracker with a triage decision before the pack is signed |
| A vendor model is in the change and the pack is silent on the vendor | No shared-responsibility split (p. 5) | Write which party does each relevant task and how each attests |
| The pack has no *not covered* section | The Profile expects one (p. 4); a pack that claims full coverage of a model feature is unlikely to be true | Add the uncovered parts and the data of unknown provenance |
| The model was retrained or given new data and its tests did not rerun | PW.8.2.R2 not met | Rerun the model's tests, and check the new data's integrity first |
| A security review is treated as clearing privacy or bias | The cybersecurity-only limit (p. 5) | Route those risks to whoever handles them, and say so in the pack |

## When to Use This Reference

Reach for this source when:

- A change adds or alters a model feature (an LLM call, prompt, tool, retrieval, fine-tune or vendor model) and the builder needs the security tasks that apply, with suggested priorities.
- A model from another party is in the build and the pack must say who is responsible for what and how each attests.
- The pack claims conformance with SSDF or this Profile and needs to show what was selected and what was not covered.
- The question is whether AI-written code needs a different review bar (the Profile's answer: one bar for all code).
- The product depends on a model and needs criteria to stop using it, and a way to keep working without it.

Reach elsewhere for the base practices this Profile supplements (`nist-ssdf-1-1`), for what an attestation to those practices commits a producer to (`cisa-secure-software-attestation-form`), for the threat detail behind each LLM risk (`owasp-llm-top10-2026`), for agents acting with tools and permissions (`owasp-agentic-top10-2026`, `owasp-agentic-threats-mitigations`, `openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai`), for verifiable application security requirements at a level (`owasp-asvs-5-0`), and for whether an agent's tests are strong enough (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`). This source is guidance; it carries no measured evidence that its tasks reduce vulnerabilities.

## Worked Example

A two-person firm uses coding agents to add a triage assistant to a client's customer-support system. The assistant reads each incoming ticket, calls a vendor's hosted model, suggests a category, and in the agent's first design closes any ticket the model rates as *not an account-takeover report*. The agent reports the change done, tests green. The builder is about to assemble the warranty pack.

**What kind of change this is.** The builder is now, in the Profile's terms, an AI system producer: software that leverages a model it did not build (p. ii). The model's inputs are customer tickets, written by anyone. The Profile's starting point applies directly:

> "A unique challenge for this community is the blurring of traditional boundaries between system code and system data, as well as the use of plain human language as the means of interaction with the systems." [V]

(p. 1). The ticket text is input to a system that takes instructions in plain language, so triage cannot stop at the diff (Concept 3).

**Triage.** The reviewer agent runs the risk model against the AI threat types in PW.1.1.R1: unwanted content in inputs and outputs, unauthorised information disclosure, supply chain. Then PW.1.1.C2: the model is on a critical path for a significant security decision, since a missed account-takeover report closes itself. The gate action: no auto-close; a human confirms any closure the model proposes for a ticket mentioning login, password or account access (Concept 4). The builder records which Profile tasks were selected for this change and which were left out as not applying (no training, no fine-tuning, so PW.3 is out), because the Profile is a starting point, not a checklist (Concept 1).

**The agent's code.** The builder is tempted to treat the agent's tests as the evaluation. The Profile does not distinguish human-written from AI-generated code, "because it is assumed that all source code should be evaluated for vulnerabilities and other issues before use" [V] (p. 2). So the code goes through the same gates as any change: static analysis with every finding recorded and triaged in the tracker (PW.7.2), and the model feature brought under testing with use case and adversarial cases, such as tickets that carry instructions to the model (PW.8.1.R1), automated as regression tests (PW.8.1.C1). Inputs are logged, validated and sanitised, and outputs encoded so nothing the model returns executes (PW.5.1). The agent also added a client library for the vendor's API; it is verified like any acquired component before it stays (PW.4.4) (Concepts 6, 7, 9).

**The vendor.** The builder cannot inspect the vendor's weights or training data. The Profile expects that split to be written down: an agreement setting out

> "which party is responsible for each practice and task and how each party will attest to its conformance with the agreement" [V]

(p. 5). The pack names what the vendor attests to (from its published terms), what the firm does, and lists the vendor model's training data and weights under *not covered*, as the Profile asks for parts the practices do not reach (p. 4; Concept 11).

**Stop criteria and the pack.** Before release, the builder sets the criteria for switching the assistant off (a confirmed prompt-injection route, or misrouted account-takeover reports above a stated count) and keeps manual triage as the fallback:

> "Consider being prepared to stop using an AI model at any time and to continue operations through other means until the AI model’s risks are sufficiently addressed." [V]

(RV.2.2.C1, p. 19; Concept 12). The pack carries the tool artifacts for each gate (PO.3.3), the task-selection record, the vendor split, the not-covered list, the stop criteria, and one line saying that its evidence covers cybersecurity only: the privacy of ticket contents is handled separately (p. 5). Deployment and operation sit outside the Profile, so the rollout itself is warranted from other sources.

## Anti-patterns This Reference Helps Avoid

- **Conformance as a badge.** Signal: *follows 800-218A* on the pack with no task list. Diagnosis: the Profile is not a checklist and says not all tasks apply to all uses (p. 4). Follow-up: record the selection and the reasons.
- **The model as the security gate.** Signal: a model's output grants, closes or approves something security-relevant, unattended. Diagnosis: PW.1.1.C2's critical-path check skipped. Follow-up: add the human step or record why the risk model does not need one.
- **A lighter bar for agent code.** Signal: *the agent wrote tests and they pass* offered in place of the review or analysis other code gets. Diagnosis: the Profile holds all source code to evaluation before use (p. 2). Follow-up: run the same gates, recorded.
- **Findings left in the conversation.** Signal: review or scan output summarised by the agent and never filed. Diagnosis: PW.7.2 and PW.8.2 record and triage every issue in the tracker. Follow-up: file and triage before sign-off.
- **The vendor as a black box nobody wrote down.** Signal: a hosted model in the change and no line on what its producer attests. Diagnosis: the shared responsibility model unrecorded (p. 5). Follow-up: write the per-task split and the uncovered parts.
- **Full coverage claimed.** Signal: no *not covered* section. Diagnosis: the Profile names parts of a model that resist secure-development practice and asks for them to be documented (p. 4). Follow-up: list them, with data of unknown provenance (PW.3.2).
- **No way to stop.** Signal: the product cannot run without the model, and nobody has said what would make them switch it off. Diagnosis: RV.2.2.R2 and C1 unmet. Follow-up: write the criteria and the fallback before release.
- **Security evidence stretched to cover other risks.** Signal: a clean scan read as clearing privacy or bias concerns. Diagnosis: the Profile addresses cybersecurity risk only (p. 5). Follow-up: route the other risks and say so.

## Integration with Other References

| Reference | Relationship |
|---|---|
| `nist-ssdf-1-1` | The base this Profile supplements and "should not be used without" [V] (p. 1). Same four practice groups and the same not-a-checklist stance. Two traps when reading them together. PW.3 in SSDF 1.1 is a retired identifier whose tasks moved to PW.4 and PO.1.3; in this Profile PW.3 is a new practice on training-data integrity, so a bare *PW.3* means different things in the two. And PW.2.1 differs (named below). Where this Profile says *No additions to SSDF 1.1*, SSDF 1.1's notional examples are the guidance |
| `cisa-secure-software-attestation-form` | The form attests to four practices derived from SP 800-218. This Profile adds the model-specific tasks on top of those practices, and its shared-responsibility agreement (each party's tasks and how each attests) is where a builder using a vendor's model splits what can be attested |
| `owasp-llm-top10-2026` | The Profile's *OWASP:* references are identifiers in Top 10 for LLM Applications Version 1.1, which the 2026 list's revision history records as an earlier version. The 2026 list numbers its risks differently (its LLM03 is Excessive Agency, LLM04 Supply Chain, LLM05 Data and Model Poisoning), so the Profile's identifiers must not be read against it. Use the 2026 list for the threat detail (unsigned model artifacts, inventories extended to models) and the Profile for the development tasks that answer it (PS.2.1, PS.3.2, PW.4.4) |
| `owasp-agentic-top10-2026`, `owasp-agentic-threats-mitigations` | They carry what the Profile does not: agents acting with tools, least privilege per agent tool, human approval for high-impact actions. The Profile's human-in-the-loop items concern security checks and security decisions inside model development. Combine at Phases 2 and 4 |
| `openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai` | Agrees on root causes and fixing the class rather than the instance (RV.3), and on recording findings. Carries the agent-harness controls the Profile lacks (sandboxing matched to capability, gates enforced outside the AI). Named tension on whether AI-written code needs its own bar (below) |
| `uk-duck-book-qa-of-code` | Both require code to be evaluated before use. The Duck Book adds a rule specific to LLM-generated code (the person who generated it reviews it and is responsible for it); the Profile adds none. Combine at Phases 6 and 7 for who answers for the agent's code |
| `owasp-asvs-5-0` | The application's own security requirements at a stated level; the Profile adds the model-development requirements to them (PO.1.2.R1). Combine at Phases 1 and 2 |
| `egashira-testsuitebench-2026` | The Profile brings models under testing policy and names test types but says nothing about who writes the tests or how strong an agent's tests are; this source measures that. Combine at Phase 3 |

**Named tensions and disagreements.**

- *Design review: both, or either.* SSDF 1.1's PW.2.1 has the design reviewed by qualified people not involved with it and/or by automated processes in the toolchain (`nist-ssdf-1-1`). This Profile tags its PW.2.1 *Modified from SSDF 1.1* and reads 1) a qualified person not involved with the design *and* 2) automated processes (PW.2.1, p. 14). For a model feature, automation alone does not meet the Profile's version.
- *One bar, or an AI-specific one.* The Profile does not distinguish AI-generated from human-written source code, since all code should be evaluated before use (p. 2). `openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai` treats AI-written code as its own case: AI often generates insecure code, so where failures could be serious it should not be accepted without human review, while code with no possible security impact may be fine unreviewed. `owasp-agentic-threats-mitigations` likewise flags AI-generated code running with elevated privileges for manual review. A tension rather than a contradiction: the Profile does not say what the evaluation must be, and the other two say where AI-written code needs a human.

## Citation and Source-Integrity Notes

**Borrowed-through gaps.** The Profile answers Executive Order 14110 and supplements SP 800-218, held here as `nist-ssdf-1-1`. Its threat-type examples (PW.1.1.R1) are cited from NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy; its informative references point to NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications Version 1.1 and that taxonomy; its artifact and evidence definitions and its exploratory-data-analysis pointer come from other NIST publications. None of these is held in this corpus except SSDF 1.1; the OWASP list is held only in its 2026 edition, which numbers its risks differently. All are `[BT]`. The informative-reference identifiers are not reproduced in this distillation.

**Named limits of the source.** Cybersecurity risk only; privacy, intellectual property and bias are to be managed elsewhere (p. 5). Deployment and operation of AI systems are out of scope (p. 2), as is most of the data governance life cycle (pp. 2, 8). Written for model producers, system producers and acquirers, not for coding agents; its statement on AI-generated code is the only direct one. Its items are recommendations, considerations and notes to be adapted or omitted, with suggested priorities. Ten tasks carry *No additions to SSDF 1.1*, so SSDF 1.1 is the guidance there. NIST is considering an Implementation Examples column for a future version (p. 7), a re-projection trigger.

**Evidence-marker continuity.** Every quotation marked `[V]` is copied from a `[V]` passage in the deep reference, which passed Pass I on 2026-10-15. The three blockquotes in the worked example are `[V]` passages in the deep reference; the shared-responsibility one is a fragment, introduced by the distillation's own words outside the quotation marks. Item-level paraphrases keep the deep reference's `[AP]`; the threat-type list and the artifact definitions keep `[BT]`. The PW.2.1 *and* is the deep reference's `[AP]` paraphrase of the task text; the comparison with SSDF 1.1's *and/or* rests on the two deep references.

## Runtime triggers this source addresses

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The change adds an LLM call, a prompt, a tool an agent can call, or memory | AI threat types in risk modelling (PW.1.1.R1); no model on a critical security path without a human (PW.1.1.C2); input and output handling (PW.5.1); acquired-model verification (PW.4.4) (Concepts 3, 4, 9) | Run the risk model against the AI threat types before the build, and check whether the model's output decides anything security-relevant on its own. |
| The change stores or moves personal data | Sensitive data used in model development, including production data, only in approved environments (PO.5.1.R2); models trained on sensitive data tracked, with access possibly limited (PS.3.2.R2); existing data classification reused (PO.1.2.C1). Privacy itself is outside the Profile (p. 5) | If the data goes near a model, classify it and keep it in approved places; the privacy question still needs its own owner. |
| The change is business-critical, or complex enough that nobody can predict its effects | Risk, cost, feasibility and applicability decide which tasks to use and how much effort each gets (p. 4); risk-proportionate practices (PS.1.3.R4); some models too complex to inspect thoroughly (p. 1) (Concept 1) | Select more of the Profile's tasks and give them more effort here, and record the selection. |
| The suite takes minutes, so it runs rarely | Consider automating tests in the pipeline as regression tests (PW.8.1.C1); rely mainly on automation for ongoing scanning and testing (RV.1.2.R2) (Concept 7) | Put the model's tests in the pipeline so they run on every change, not when someone remembers. |
| The agent's environment can reach production credentials or data | Separate environments; production data only in approved environments; least privilege; continuous plaintext-secrets monitoring (PO.5.1.C1, R2, R3, R6) (Concept 8; transfer) | Take the production data and credentials out of the agent's reach, and keep a watch for plaintext secrets running. |
| The agent reads untrusted content (web pages, issues, emails) while holding tools | Blurred code/data boundary and plain-language interaction; crafted queries driving injection-style attacks (p. 1); inputs logged, validated and sanitised, outputs encoded (PW.5.1.R2–R3) (transfer for the agent itself) | Treat what the model reads as input from an attacker; validate it going in and encode what comes out. |
| The agent adds a dependency nobody asked for | Verify acquired components against requirements throughout their life cycles, and an acquired model's integrity, provenance and security before use (PW.4.4); track provenance (PS.3.2) (Concept 9) | Verify it before it stays: where it came from, that it is what it claims to be, and that it is free of known flaws. |
| The agent runs for an hour unattended and reports success | Tools configured to generate artifacts as evidence of the practices (PO.3.3) (Concept 5) | The report is a claim; the tool's own record is the evidence. Attach the record. |
| A gate was skipped "just this once" | Justify any case where requirements are relaxed or waived (PW.1); define and track criteria for security checks (PO.4.1) | A skip is a waiver: write the justification on the pack, or run the gate. |
| Lint and type errors are suppressed rather than fixed | Record and triage all discovered issues and recommended remediations in the tracker (PW.7.2) (Concept 6) | Each suppression is a discovered issue: file it and triage it. |
| The secrets scan or dependency audit is "noisy" so it was turned off | Continuously monitor each environment for plaintext secrets (PO.5.1.R6); verify components throughout their life cycles (PW.4.4); monitor vulnerability databases (RV.1.1.R3) | The Profile says *continuously*; turn it back on and triage the noise. |
| The same session that wrote the code reviews it | Design reviewed by a qualified person not involved with it and by automation (PW.2.1) (Concept 10; transfer from design review to change review) | The author is not the reviewer; route it to one who had no part in the design, and keep the automated checks as well. |
| The reviewer's findings are long and nobody sorts them | Record and triage all discovered issues and recommended remediations (PW.7.2, PW.8.2) (Concept 6) | Every finding goes in the tracker with a triage decision; none stays in the transcript. |
| The builder approves because reading the diff is too slow | Code review and/or code analysis chosen by policy (PW.7.1); automated toolchains ideally do most of the work (PO.3.1.N1); all code evaluated before use, AI-generated or not (p. 2) (Concepts 2, 6) | Not reading the diff is a choice of analysis over review: record it, and show the analysis ran. |
| The change "looks fine" but touches something with a history of incidents | Analyse root causes over time for patterns; review for similar vulnerabilities to eradicate the class (RV.3.2, RV.3.3) (Concept 12) | Check the root-cause record for this area first, and look for the same class in the change. |
| The pack says "all tests pass" with no run record | Artifacts as evidence (PO.3.3); test results documented and issues recorded (PW.8.2) (Concept 5) | No artifact, no pass: send it back for the run record. |
| A risk is listed with no owner and no rollback | Criteria and processes for when to stop using a model and when to roll back (RV.2.2.R2); roles cover all parts of the SDLC (PO.2.1) (Concept 12) | For a model risk, name the stop criteria, the rollback and who decides, before signing. |
| Something went wrong after release | Analyse the vulnerability's risk, including deep analysis of model input and output (RV.2.1); root cause, patterns, class sweep, process update (RV.3) (Concept 12) | Find the root cause, sweep for the class, and change the process so it does not recur. |
